moves: Declares the Supreme Lord's procedure of consecration (abhiṣeka), identified as putraka-dīkṣā, fit to join a person to categories that are objects of enjoyment.
Cites Kāmika and Siddhayogīśvarīmata to stress that adhva-sandhāna is required for true spiritual preceptorship, not mere consecration through succession.
States that non-men, women, śūdras, and others desiring it are not to be scrutinized at initiation; investigation belongs at the time of knowledge.
Prescribes sprinkling the disciple sixty-four times, then once with water full of the sap of the mantras, with might and greatness.
Explains that the former guru, having abandoned authority, is unbound, since spiritual lineage is like a lamp kindled from a lamp; transmission must not be broken before death.
Authorizes the guru regarding four tasks and enjoins protection of seven sacrifices, including initiation, explanation, compassion, friendship, and giving food.
Requires delivery of all instruments, such as knife and chalk, to the learned disciple during consecration.
Clarifies that no adhikāra assignment or vow of knowledge is conferred here; what is conferred is the sādhya-mantra, and all instruction is delivery of one's own instruments.

Contextualizes with Dupuche's Kula-ritual material: ordinary samaya-dīkṣā is a prelude; putraka initiation has types; śivahasta consecration; hierarchy of kalpita/akalpita guru; and Dyczkowski's note that TĀ 23 concerns teacher consecration while TĀ 24 concerns funerary rites.
traps: Do not conflate TĀ 23 with Dupuche's Kula-ritual consecration material or with TĀ 29's putraka initiation types; they are related but not identical targets.
Do not confuse samaya-dīkṣā (ordinary initiation) with putraka-dīkṣā/abhiṣeka (consecration as teacher).
Do not conflate kalpita guru (consecrated by rite) with akalpita guru (directly empowered); the excerpts distinguish them.
Do not treat the Kāmika citation as a full Kāmika Āgama exposition; it is only a cited authority in TĀ 23.
